ai-at-work.title: Anthropic reportedly plans to move forward with IPO plans
ai-at-work.excerpt: The AI company is expected to set its valuation range this week, the Wall Street Journal reported.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic is gearing up for an IPO by setting its valuation range this week, according to reports. Digital workplace leaders need to pay attention because AI infrastructure decisions made by well-funded public companies directly shape the tools and platforms we'll be deploying in our organizations over the next five years. Here's the thing though: another AI company going public doesn't automatically mean your Slack integration will get smarter, so don't let the IPO theater distract you from actually testing whether Claude or ChatGPT actually solves your real workplace problems.

ai-at-work.title: Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy puts Nvidia’s China ambitions under scrutiny
ai-at-work.excerpt: Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy threatens to complicate Nvidia’s lobbying efforts to loosen U.S. chip export restrictions and maintain access to China’s lucrative AI market.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang is reportedly involved with someone alleged to have Chinese intelligence connections, which is now creating headaches for the company's efforts to navigate U.S. export controls and keep selling chips to China. For digital workplace folks, this is a reminder that executive behavior and personal choices don't stay personal anymore, they affect corporate strategy, compliance posture, and how seriously regulators take your company's requests. Nothing says "we're trustworthy with sensitive tech" like a geopolitical scandal wrapped around your CEO's personal life.

ai-at-work.title: Anthropic joins AI’s natural gas frenzy, buys $3.4B worth of turbines
ai-at-work.excerpt: Anthropic bought billions of dollars' worth of natural gas turbines in a deal that could give it buyer's remorse.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic just dropped $3.4 billion on natural gas turbines to power its AI infrastructure, betting big that they need serious baseload energy for the long haul. This matters because it signals that AI companies are finally waking up to the infrastructure reality: you can't run massive language models on wishes and venture capital alone. Here's the thing though, if your AI company needs to lock in decade-long energy commitments before you've actually proven your product makes money, you might want to ask yourself some harder questions than just how many GPUs you can cram into a data center.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft’s email security is unexpectedly blocking legitimate business mail
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft’s email filters meant to protect users from malicious messages appear to be rejecting legitimate ones. Over the last few days, some mail sent to Microsoft consumer addresses have bounced if
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft's email filters started rejecting legitimate business emails to Outlook and Hotmail addresses because senders lacked proper DMARC authentication records. This matters because email deliverability directly impacts workplace productivity and external communications, so IT teams need to scramble through authentication compliance to avoid frustrated executives wondering where their messages went. After three decades watching email drama unfold, I can tell you this is peak Microsoft: solving a real security problem by creating a worse problem for everyone else.

digital-culture.title: No one knows how to dress for work anymore—even executives
digital-culture.excerpt: Companies spent years dragging employees back to the office, but forgot to tell them what to wear. The result is confusion stretching from junior employees to the executive suite. One of Grant Alexand
digital-culture.dwp_take: Companies yanked everyone back to offices without establishing clear dress codes, leaving everyone from entry-level staff to C-suite executives genuinely confused about what to wear. This matters because unclear expectations create anxiety, undermine confidence, and waste mental energy on something that should be a solved problem, especially when you're trying to focus on actual work. The fact that a COO is getting wardrobe questions from VPs tells you everything you need to know: leadership forgot that going back to the office means going back to shared norms, not just shared square footage.

digital-culture.dwp_take: Mastercard's CEO Michael Miebach apparently discovered that getting people to actually work together beats the old command-and-control playbook. digital-culture.excerpt: The Nvidia CEO began working with consultants from Heller as early as October 2025, around the same time he was first linked to a suspected Chinese spy.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Jensen Huang brought in a crisis PR firm just as questions were swirling about alleged ties to Chinese intelligence operations. For digital workplace leaders, this is a reminder that your CEO's problems become your company culture problems fast, whether through internal chatter, recruitment headwinds, or trust erosion with partners and customers. Nothing says "we've got this under control" quite like quietly hiring the scandal specialists while denying there's a scandal to begin with.
